blocks.text: Locke was deeply resentful of this unwanted publicity for his Essay. He was especially resentful of the fact that Stillingfleet had grouped him alongside the reviled Toland as one of 'the Gentlemen of the new way of reasoning' who had undermined the articles of the Christian faith. Stillingfleet's name carried considerable weight and authority in this period: as the author of several popular works, he was better known and more widely respected than Locke, a relative newcomer to the field. As a consequence, Locke was compelled to clear his name. His first response to Stillingfleet was A Letter To the Right Reverend Edward Lord Bishop of Worcester (1697), complaining that he had been unfairly vilified by association. He accused Stillingfleet of failing to read his work carefully and charitably, independently of Toland's views. Stillingfleet responded to Locke with his defiant Answer to Mr. Locke's Letter (dated March 1697), then Locke issued an equally defiant Reply (June 1697). Stillingfleet fought back with his second Answer (September 1697), and Locke issued a further 452-page Reply (May 1698). Finally, Stillingfleet died in 1699 and the dispute came to an end.

blocks.text: The following correspondence shows that in the middle of this controversy stood Elizabeth Burnet (then Berkeley), friend to both writers and deeply disturbed by the lack of charity being shown on both sides. In one of her first letters (4.1.2), she hints that Locke had become annoyed at some remarks that Stillingfleet had made in a personal letter to Burnet. It is likely that Stillingfleet's remarks were about Locke's first Letter in the debate—a possible catalyst for Locke's next Reply to Stillingfleet. Burnet tries to dispel Locke's annoyance by taking the blame on herself: she might have misread Stillingfleet's point, she suggests, and presented it in a bad light. She reassures Locke that Stillingfleet holds him in great esteem and respect, and pleads with Locke to be 'charitable' and 'just' toward his adversary.

blocks.text: Burnet's efforts were in vain. In late August or early September that year, Locke published his Reply to Stillingfleet and sent Burnet a bound presentation copy. At Locke's request, in her letter of 22 September 1697 (4.1.4), Burnet provides a lengthy 'reflection' on this work. Quite candidly, she tells Locke that it would be best for him to remain silent in future. He is too quick to take personal offence, he has been unfair and uncharitable to Stillingfleet, and his comments are often irrelevant and pernickety. She expresses a hope that he might use his philosophical skill to find points of agreement with Stillingfleet in future, and to show greater 'generosity and disinterestness' toward his opponent.

blocks.text: Burnet's reflections demonstrate that she is a philosophically astute reader of this dispute. In his Reply to Stillingfleet, Locke is at pains to emphasize that his way of reasoning differs from that of Toland: while Toland makes clear and distinct ideas a prerequisite for certainty, Locke asserts that certainty consists in the perception of the agreement or disagreement of ideas whether or not those ideas are clear and distinct. In response, Burnet points out that Stillingfleet impugns not only Toland's way of certainty by clear and distinct ideas, but also Locke's way of certainty by the agreement and disagreement of ideas. Both criteria of certainty potentially lead to scepticism and irreligion, in the bishop's view. To settle the dispute, Burnet suggests, it is not enough for Locke simply to distinguish his position from that of Toland. Instead, Locke might emphasize to Stillingfleet that he (Locke) does not require certainty in order to assent to matters of faith. In his Essay (III.xviii.2), Locke asserts that faith consists simply in assent to propositions based on the credit of the proposer as coming from God (divine revelation), not on reason. From this viewpoint, lack of certainty in our ideas (of substance, person, essence, and so forth) does not necessarily threaten belief in the articles of the Christian faith.

In the opening programmatic statement of the Essay, Locke declares that his main objective is to help readers attain contentment and satisfaction with the knowledge that they have available to them in their current state (that is, as embodied human subjects). blocks.text: The topic of cultivating this virtuous disposition is reiterated in Burnet's Method of Devotion. The main purpose of her religious instruction book is to bring young and under-educated readers (namely women) to self-knowledge through careful, methodical self-examination. Above all, she recommends that her readers acquire a standing disposition to pray to God and to show loving kindness toward one another. This loving kindness consists in a habitual tendency to judge others charitably, and it is facilitated by freedom from the slavery of selfish appetites and passions. $ ^{8} $ In her view, one should uphold a charitable disposition in the midst of philosophical disputation. In passages that may be a commentary on the Locke-Stillingfleet exchange, she says that 'to dwell long on some Speculations, such as the Disputes of Predestination, of the Trinity, the Union of the Divine and Humane Nature, and the like; such obscure Inquiries, beyond the plain Doctrine as delivered in the Scriptures, are not proper Subjects of Meditation'. If you must dispute, she suggests, then it is better done with a calm and cool head, without prepossession or prejudice, and with a spirit of charity toward others' differences. $ ^{9} $ If you see that your adversary has truth on his side, then you must sincerely acknowledge this. $ ^{10} $ If your adversary is unfair and disingenuous toward you, then it is advisable to dismiss the dispute till your inflamed passion has subsided. for, at least very unwillingly undergo; but it will be more to my advantage in preserving those favourable thoughts you have too hastely intertained of me, if you will take my advise and not read the inclosed at all but burn or return it me again, I having hardly had time to read, I'm sure not to consider it as I ought before I troubled you with it; however I have observed your request $ ^{28} $ in taking a fredom that is not pardonable but as a proof of sincerity. 'Tis not hard to express esteem where wee really find wee have it, and 'tis much easier making excuses for my own defects of which I'm so aboundantly sinsable; by sending a letter so faulty in sense, English, and so on, I know I expose my ignorance, but I would be so humble to be content to be thought on as I am; I am sure a complement though never so justly turned, could be of no service, and if the inclosed is as useless It is because I cant tell how to make any letter from me any otherwise. My intention has ben good and you must excuse the performance. I am not quite of your mind as to the necessity of your vindication, $ ^{29} $ you owe it perhaps to your self and in that respect it is reasonable and fitt, but all things considered could you be content to dispence with your own right I think it would be most charitable and best to be silant; their being not a great many able and fewer willing to make a good and right use of this dispute. I hear my Lord has some thoughts of writing, $ ^{30} $ but hope he will not, not having heard him speak of doing it, or of your Book, which I was glad of 'till I had sent this, that I might be the less biased, had I had opportunity to hear proper Judges discours of your Book my letter might have had fewer of such week inquieries, but you love to convers with childeren and see the naturall productions of the mind, unasisted by art, and unposest by others notions, mine is too much so, which will I hope be an apoligie for the defects as well as pl[ain] $ ^{31} $ dealing of
Sir
Your Faithfull servent
[Her enclosure, fols. 210-11:]
E. B.

blocks.text: Being on a journy when your Book came first out I neither gott the favour of that you were pleased to send me $ ^{32} $ nor time to read any other, indid I took one in sheets $ ^{33} $ as I went throw Oxford and read great part of it but twas with so many inturptions, that I was willing to give it a second reading which has deferred my <thanks> $ ^{34} $ longer then my obligations would otherwise have allowed; you have indid put the tryall $ ^{35} $ of my Frindship on a pretty hard service not only in respect of my ignorance which is not my fault but misfortune, but in respect of the persons consarned in the dispute, $ ^{36} $ and I can't tell how I could be impartial did not the esteem I have for both make me so, but to satisfy you 'tis not lasyness or unwillingness to obey you I have sett down some reflections I made in my second reading your Book, which is the best way to convince you how incapable I am of being any more so tasked, being in a Frinds House I have not so much command of my time, or if I had should perhaps want skill to shorten this letter by using any other method then taking the Book as I read it and referring you to the pages by which I hope you'll gess my meaning though am sorry to give you so much trouble to so little purpose; but being your own fault I ought to be excused at least forgiven. In severall places of your Book I thought you were a litle too Criticall in observeing small faults in the exactness of writing that did not imediatly relate to your self or matter of your complaint, to correct such errors in a Frind is kind and allowable, or to expose a vain pretender to knowledg, but my Lords reputation for larning is so justly established and of so publick a benefit, that all needless reflections ought to be avoided, sinse'tis of less ill consequence to have it thought you mistook my L[ord] then that my L[ord] mistook the truth; and had you more willingly used your art to clear what was I owne too obscure in my Lords books then to make that obscurity more observable, you might I fancy have found less disagreement in your Ideas, and don what well became the generosity and disinterestness of Mr Locke though it was more then the laws of a just defence obliged you to; and would both sides but take the same pains to find wherin they mean alike as they do to show wherin they defer or mistake truth in their maner of defending it, I can't but believe the oposistion would be reduced to a few perticulers; and the rest found only a dispute of words that seem to clash when both intend

But considering how little time I have for soe long a Letter as that would be, and how much I should trespass upon your time in it, I thought it better to reserve it till I have the honour to wait upon you in Town. When I discourse with you on those points I shall see how far you allow of my reasons: And where I finde you continue to think me in an error I shall know what use to make of it another time. But it would be to presume too much on your $ ^{84} $ to expect those answers from you in writeing, which I may hope from a personall conversation with you: And it would ill become me to put you to such a penance for my advantage. I am too, often troubled with gideness and disorders in my head, so that my memorie and the exercis of my mind is much broken and confused, which indid makes me most desireous to find some remedy since the other pains and inconveniancys are not so great but I could very well baer them; I am sinsible I have an exceeding sharp humer in my stomack, and if I eat much butter or the like it will rise like greas for a long time, being allso often troubled both with hart burn and a palpatation; in this maner I am, and have been for severall years, from about midsumer to Christmas, and by that time my apetite to my meat go's away so intirely that no variety or any sort of food gos down with pleasure, but quit the Contrary tis very troublesome to force my self to eat, and this lose of apetite lasts 'till about May or June, but the litle I eat seems to digest pretty well, I then grow very leane, wake generally sick, and with a great sadness and opression on my spirits as after some great misfortune; blocks.text: what I take the fredom to ask is not a direction to any sort of Medicen, but only some few rules for my deat that may best moderate these uneasyness especially those disorders of my head, and spirits, and disposition to sadness which makes me a very dull useless creature; shall I contenew to abstain from wine or not; is much excercise necesary, for I own I use very litle; is Chocolet bad and Coffe; for air I find litle diference in Town or Country of the two I think the last best; but afected by chang of weather: before rain and especially snow I am much worse; and cold very ill agrees with me; if you are so well as to be able without any uneasyness to write five or six lines in answer to this very long and impertenat leter it will be very acceptable, because I find a particular satisfaction in observeing the rules of one for whom I have so much deference, and pray dont fear being too severe, since I value nothing in meat or drink but in order to health, and can without grife deny my self any thing of that sort? blocks.text: imployments would have taught me a reasonable distance, but since their was in your last something requierd (which is to me a Command) it makes it like a fault to obey so slowly. I own were it not from you, I should suspect it a complement you thought I expected, when you bid me send the papers I mentioned; $ ^{110} $ but I am perswaded you never misleade those who depend on you, or bid them do what you disaprove if they obey; therefore without more niceness I now send them, and had don it some time since had I not ben without one days health some time before I had your letter and ever since, I think I begen to mend a litle though slowly; I fond by reading then lately (when my first thoughts were out of memorie) the sense very obscure (if'tis not too much to suppose any part disarves to be called even dark or confused sense) I can but just find my own meening and doute much if a stranger to my thoughts can often find any meening at all, besides the trouble they will give in reading for want of setting down the Texts in words at lenth, this made me purpose to writt them over mending at least the last fault and leveing out some less probable Texts; $ ^{111} $ but though I began I was so ill and so listless I could not go on; I send them because you bid me, but do not ask their reading. They are not worth your time; I thank you for your very obliging letter, and good advise; I am too sensible both of my want of Judgment and information to believe those who differ from me must be in eror; the contrary is a fault I more incline to; concluding I am wrong when I can not easyly think as others do, and were I not some times incourged by finding persones whos goodness and knowledg I esteem in the same sentiments, I should be very defident; the severe and sensorious side is so contrary to my temper, that it is rather a prejudice then an alurment to that side; as I had only the Bible when I writ the inclosed papers, so I have not since consulted farther, but 'tis most probable the sense I have given is only what I have heard or read and has insenseable stuck to my memorie; Thank God I am not uneasyly curious about what is obscurely revelled either with respect to what is future or in other matters above our clear and full comprehension; I look on the scripture more as a rule of life in order to a future and better state, then a designed information of the Nature of that happeness; and if I can but rightly understand and Honestly perform my part, I shall I hope quietly comit my future
